content.title: About
content.content: Beef liver is the organ meat of cattle, packed with nutrients. It has a tender, slightly bitter flavor and a soft texture when cooked. Liver is a staple in many traditional cuisines and can be pan‑fried, stewed, baked, or made into pâtés.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef liver is one of the most concentrated sources of vitamin A in foods.
In the 19th century liver was considered “food for the strong” and was a common part of athletes’ and laborers’ diets.
The iron in liver is in the highly bioavailable heme form, easier for the body to absorb than plant iron.
In some cultures liver is served as a delicacy, but unlike foie gras it does not require special fattening of the animal.
Liver loses nutrients quickly after slaughter, so it is best eaten fresh.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: High in iron
items.content: Heme iron helps form hemoglobin and prevents anemia.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Liver provides B12, riboflavin, niacin, and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Liver offers complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains copper and zinc
items.content: These minerals support enzyme function, immunity, and wound healing.

items.title: High vitamin A content
items.content: Excessive liver consumption can lead to hypervitaminosis A, especially in pregnant women.

items.title: Cholesterol level
items.content: Liver is relatively high in cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should limit intake.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Liver can accumulate toxins and heavy metals, so choose products from reputable sources.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef liver.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Liver can be quickly sautéed with onions, made into pâté, added to stews or soups. Before cooking, rinse it, remove any membranes, and cut into bite‑size pieces. For a milder taste, many chefs marinate liver in milk or lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh beef liver in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for about 3 months. Before use, check for an off‑odor – a sour or rancid smell indicates spoilage.
